paper_title: GLOW-FM: Efficient Generative Low-Light Image Enhancement with One-Step Latent Flow Matching

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) aims to recover well-exposed and perceptually faithful images from severely degraded observations. Recent diffusion-based generative methods achieve strong perceptual quality by leveraging powerful image priors, but their iterative sampling incurs substantial computational cost, limiting practical deployment. Despite recent efficiency gains in generative LLIE, high-quality enhancement with a single function evaluation and low overall computation remains challenging, particularly under diverse real-world low-light conditions. We introduce GLOW-FM, a one-step latent flow-matching framework for efficient generative LLIE. GLOW-FM performs conditional transport in the latent space of a frozen Tiny-VAE and leverages Terminal Velocity Matching (TVM) to enable enhancement with a single function evaluation. Matched comparisons with alternative one-step objectives support TVM as an effective design choice, and, to the best of our knowledge, this is its first adaptation to image restoration and specifically to LLIE. Extensive experiments on challenging real-world benchmarks demonstrate that GLOW-FM achieves competitive image quality and state-of-the-art cross-dataset generalization while requiring only a single function evaluation and 34 GFLOPs for the small variant. These findings highlight the potential of GLOW-FM to bring generative LLIE closer to practical deployment through single-step inference and compact latent modeling. Code will be made publicly available upon publication.

Code is available at https://github.com/armresearch/AAIR-GLOW-FM. 1. Introduction image enhancement Low-light (LLIE) aims to recover well-exposed and visually pleasing images from observations captured under insufficient illumination. Real-world low-light images often exhibit complex combination of degradations, including severe underexposure, sensor noise, color distortion, reduced contrast, detail loss, and local saturation, which vary significantly across cameras and imaging conditions, making LLIE challenging problem in real-world imaging [6, 8, 28]. Consequently, LLIE seeks not only to enhance image appearance but also to restore perceptually faithful content that supports reliable high-level vision applications [16, 40]. Regression-based LLIE methods provide strong distortion performance and efficient inference [4, 5, 7, 45, 54, 58, 59, 61, 62, 68, 69]. These approaches typically optimize distortionoriented objectives and are effective at recovering visibility and suppressing noise, but often struggle under severe degradation, where substantial information loss makes enhancement inherently ambiguous. Trained with pixel-wise objectives, they tend to produce overly smooth results and suppress fine details [3]. To address this limitation, generative models [17, 19, 21, 22, 55, 65, 66] have emerged as powerful LLIE paradigm, learning the distribution of natural images and leveraging strong image 1 priors to recover realistic textures and structures that are difficult to reconstruct with deterministic networks. These methods demonstrate substantial improvements in perceptual quality and robustness under severe degradations. However, these gains come at the cost of iterative sampling, resulting in high computational complexity and limiting practical deployment, particularly for high-resolution enhancement in resource-constrained applications such as smartphone camera image processing. To address this limitation, several efficient generative LLIE frameworks have recently been proposed [20, 25, 70]. These methods significantly reduce the required number of function evaluations (NFEs) compared to conventional diffusion models. Nevertheless, they still rely on iterative refinement procedures and diffusion-inspired architectures whose computational complexity remains substantial. For example, WCDM [20] requires 10 NFEs and approximately 90 GFLOPs during inference, while ReDDiT [25] reduces sampling to 2 NFEs but still requires roughly 128 GFLOPs. Consequently, while recent generative LLIE approaches have substantially reduced sampling cost, achieving high-quality enhancement with single inference step and low overall computational budget remains an active challenge, particularly across diverse and demanding real-world low-light conditions. In this work, we address this challenge by introducing an efficient Generative Low-Light image enhancement with one-step latent Flow Matching (GLOW-FM). Our approach leverages Terminal Velocity Matching (TVM) [71], which enables direct prediction of the normal-light image, eliminating the need for iterative sampling during inference. Comparisons with standard Flow Matching [30, 31], Consistency Flow Matching [63], and MeanFlow [12] establish Terminal Velocity Matching (TVM) [71] as deliberate design choice for single-step LLIE. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first adaptation of TVM to image restoration, and specifically to LLIE. GLOW-FM learns conditional transport that maps degraded low-light representations directly to their well-exposed counterparts in the latent space of frozen Tiny-VAE [49]. Operating in this compact latent space substantially reduces computational cost while preserving the expressive power of generative modeling. Moreover, latent representations capture semantic image structure while suppressing dataset-specific variations, improving restoration and generalization [29, 48, 51]. Extensive experiments on challenging real-world low-light benchmarks [45, 54] demonstrate that GLOW-FM provides an effective generative prior for low-light enhancement while operating under small inference budgets. Despite requiring only single NFE, our method achieves image quality competitive with recent efficient generative LLIE approaches and consistently exhibits strong cross-dataset generalization as shown in Fig. 1. These results suggest that latent flow matching, combined with one-step TVM estimation, offers promising direction toward practical, high-quality, and computationally efficient low-light image enhancement. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce GLOW-FM, an efficient generative framework for low-light image enhancement (LLIE) based on latent flow matching. By performing enhancement in compact latent space with lightweight Tiny-VAE and one-step flow formulation, GLOW-FM achieves high restoration quality at low computational cost. We establish Terminal Velocity Matching (TVM) as the strongest overall one-step objective for LLIE through matched comparisons with Rectified Flow, Consistency Flow Matching, and MeanFlow. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first adaptation of TVM to image restoration, specifically LLIE. We achieve state-of-the-art cross-dataset generalization compared to generative and non-generative baselines, while maintaining competitive image quality and improved efficiency over existing generative LLIE methods. 2. Related Work 2.1. Generative Low-Light Image Enhancement large body of LLIE research focuses on directly regressing normal-light image from low-light input using Retinex decomposition [26], illumination estimation, and deep neural networks [4, 5, 45, 62]. While these approaches are computationally efficient, they often produce overly smooth results and struggle to capture the diversity of plausible normal-light reconstructions. The recent success of diffusion models [18] in image generation has motivated their adoption for high-quality low-light image enhancement [17, 1921, 25, 65, 70]. DiffRetinex [65] formulates enhancement as Retinex decomposition followed by conditional diffusion-based reconstruction of reflectance and illumination components. GSAD [19] introduces global structure-aware diffusion framework that combines curvature-based regularization with uncertainty-guided optimization to preserve scene structure and focus restoration on challenging regions. Subsequent work has largely aimed to reduce the high computational cost of diffusion sampling. ReDDiT [25] uses trajectory matching distillation in reflectance-aware residual space to reduce the NFEs required at inference. PyDiff [70] performs denoising in coarse-to-fine resolution pyramid and employs global correction module to mitigate brightness and color inconsistencies. WCDM [20] accelerates inference by conducting diffusion in the wavelet domain on low-frequency subbands while restoring high-frequency details through dedicated branch. Reti-Diff [17] generates compact latent Retinex priors to guide transformer-based restoration network, while LightenDiffusion [21] combines latent Retinex decomposition with diffusion for unsupervised LLIE. Related concurrent preprints, IllumFlow [57] and Consist-Retinex [60], further explore onestep generative LLIE through Retinex-based decomposition. 2 Figure 2. Overview of GLOW-FM Training. Paired low-light and normally exposed images are encoded into frozen autoencoder latent space. During training, the model learns both the instantaneous flow-matching velocity and terminal-velocity displacement map between arbitrary times. During inference, the enhanced latent is obtained with single step and decoded back to image space. 2.2. Generative Model Acceleration 3. Method Generative diffusion and flow models have achieved remarkable success across wide range of image-generation tasks. Their strong priors have also motivated applications to image restoration, where the goal is to recover clean image from degraded InDI [11] performs restoration through direct observation. iteration, while IR-SDE [35] models the restoration trajectory using mean-reverting stochastic process. Bridge-matching methods [46] further formalize transport between degraded and clean endpoint distributions, and flow-based approaches such as FlowIE [73] and PnP-Flow [37] extend this formulation to image restoration. Despite their strong restoration capabilities, these methods commonly require iterative sampling, resulting in substantial inference cost. Early acceleration approaches employed fast post-hoc samplers [23, 34, 47], reducing inference from hundreds of steps to tens, often at the expense of quality under aggressive acceleration. More recently, flow-based objectives have been developed specifically for efficient oneand few-step generation. Rectified Flow [31] learns straighter transport trajectories, while Consistency Flow Matching [63] regularizes the velocity field for few-step inference. ELIR [9] applies Consistency Flow Matching to image restoration in the latent space of Tiny AutoEncoder. MeanFlow [12] learns mean transport trajectories, whereas TVM [71] learns finite displacements between arbitrary timesteps for high-fidelity oneand few-step generation. Despite these advances, efficient flow-based generation remains relatively unexplored for LLIE. Building upon TVM, we introduce single-step latent flow-matching framework for efficient low-light enhancement. We formulate low-light image enhancement as conditional flow-matching problem [30] between the low-light distribution p1(x1) and the normally exposed distribution p0(x0). Given paired sample (x1,x0), where x1 p1(x1) and x0 p0(x0) denote the low-light source and normal-light target, respectively, we follow the TVM time convention [71]: the source is placed at = 1 and the target at = 0, opposite to the original Flow Matching convention. Enhancement therefore proceeds toward earlier terminal times, from t=1 to t=0. Rather than learning this transport directly in pixel space, we perform it in the latent space of frozen VAE with encoder and decoder D. We denote the corresponding latents as z1 = E(x1) and z0 = E(x0), and define intermediate states zt along the flow-path. To enable efficient inference, we train two-time conditioned model Fθ(zt,t,s) with Terminal Velocity Matching (TVM) [71], which learns displacements along the trajectory rather than relying only on numerical integration of an instantaneous velocity field. This allows the same latent flow model to support both one-step enhancement and few-step refinement. Beyond its reported strong one-step performance, we motivate TVM for restoration through theoretical analysis. Under the TVM regularity conditions [71, Theorem 1] and Lipschitz assumption on the decoder, we derive bound on the pixel-space Wasserstein-2 distance [41] between the restored-image and target normal-light distributions in terms of the TVM objectives and autoencoder reconstruction error. This links TVM training to pixel-space restoration; the complete theorem and proof are provided in Appendix B. Operating in latent space is central to the efficiency of GLOW-FM. Instead of applying the flow model to full-resolution RGB images, the VAE encoder maps the input into lower-dimensional representation with reduced spatial resolution. The learned transport therefore acts on compact latent grid, lowering the cost of each function evaluation and making low-NFE inference more practical. The latent space also provides useful restoration prior. Since the VAE is pretrained on broad natural-image distribution, its representation captures reusable image structure while suppressing some pixel-level noise and dataset-specific degradation patterns. Prior work has similarly shown that pretrained latent representations can support robust image restoration and domain generalization [29, 48, 51]. We evaluate GLOW-FM on both paired and unpaired real-world LLIE benchmarks. Our primary benchmark is LSD-DLL [45], large-scale dataset designed to improve the realism and diversity of LLIE evaluation. Unlike many earlier low-light datasets [7, 15, 64], which are limited by synthetic darkening, controlled capture settings, or restricted sensor coverage, LSD-DLL [45] provides real low and normal-light image pairs captured across diverse scenes and devices in the wild using dynamic exposure calibration and multi-frame alignment to obtain more realistic paired data. As result, it better captures phenomena such as sensor noise, spatially varying illumination, and color distortions that are often underrepresented in existing LLIE benchmarks. These properties motivated its use as the benchmark dataset in [8]. LSD-DLL also provides the LSD-U test split, which consists of unpaired low-light images captured with unseen devices and enables evaluation of generalization beyond the paired training distribution. For paired benchmarks, we evaluate both distortion and perceptual quality. Distortion is measured using PSNR and SSIM [56], while perceptual similarity is assessed using LPIPS [67]. We additionally evaluate perceptual image quality using the no-reference metrics NIQE [39] and MUSIQ [24]. For unpaired benchmarks, where ground-truth reference images are unavailable, we follow [20] and report the no-reference perceptual quality metrics NIQE [39] and BRISQUE [38]. Results are averaged over five evaluation seeds; full mean and STD results are provided in Appendix F. Implementation details. GLOW-FM employs frozen TinyVAE [49] to obtain 16-channel latent image representations, while only the latent flow model is optimized during training. Unless otherwise specified, experiments use the GLOW-FM-XL configuration with single NFE. We additionally evaluate medium (M) and small (S) configurations, which differ only in the capacity of the HDiT backbone. Source latents are perturbed with Gaussian noise using σ =0.01. Models are trained for approximately 100k optimization steps on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. For LSD-DLL and UHD-LOL4K, we trained the baselines on the respective training sets, whereas all other results use the authors official code and checkpoints. Appendix details these baseline training protocols together with our implementation, hyperparameters, and runtime and memory analyses. 4.2. Results on Paired Benchmarks Tab. 1 compares GLOW-FM with representative non-generative and recent efficient generative LLIE methods on the paired LSDDLL and UHD-LOL4K benchmarks. Across both datasets, GLOW-FM achieves favorable qualityefficiency trade-off with only single NFE during inference. On LSD-DLL, it obtains the strongest overall performance across several distortion and perceptual-quality metrics. On UHD-LOL4K, nongenerative methods remain stronger on some distortion-oriented metrics, while GLOW-FM maintains competitive image quality with substantially lower inference cost than the generative baselines. The medium and small variants further reduce computational cost while preserving strong image quality. Representative qualitative results on LSD-DLL are shown in Fig. 3. On LOL-v1, GLOW-FM maintains strong qualityefficiency tradeoff. As shown in Tab. 3, GLOW-FM achieves the best NIQE score among the compared methods with single NFE. We hypothesize that its weaker distortion performance arises from the limited training data available in this benchmark. controlled data-scaling experiment supporting this interpretation is presented in Fig. 5. Since paired evaluation does not fully capture robustness to unseen devices and low-light domains, we separately examine cross-dataset and unseen-device generalization in Sec. 4.3. 4.3. Generalization to Unseen Low-Light Data Tab. 4 reports results on five widely used unpaired real-world low-light benchmarks: DICM, LIME, MEF, NPE, and VV. Following the protocol adopted in prior work [19, 25], GLOW-FM is trained on LOL-v2-Syn [64] and evaluated directly on the target datasets without additional fine-tuning. GLOW-FM achieves the best generative NIQE and BRISQUE results on nearly all evaluated benchmarks while operating at substantially lower computational cost. It also obtains the strongest mean performance across both metrics. Tab. 2 reports results on the LSD-U subset from [8], which evaluates generalization to low-light images captured with unseen devices. Among all compared generative and non-generative methods, GLOW-FM achieves the best NIQE and MUSIQ scores with single NFE. Moreover, all GLOW-FM variants achieve competitive no-reference image quality despite substantially lower computational cost than the competing generative methods. These results demonstrate strong generalization beyond the training distribution, indicating that the proposed latent flow formulation remains robust under real-world distribution shifts. Together with the cross-dataset results in Tab. 4, they demonstrate consistent generalization across unseen devices and diverse low-light domains. 7 Figure 4. Qualitative generalization comparison. Results on unpaired real-world low-light benchmarks show that GLOW-FM recovers natural illumination while preserving scene structure across diverse inputs. Results on LSD-DLL assessing the latent representation and one-step training objective. Given the perceptiondistortion trade-off [3], we evaluate metrics from both families. Quantitative results and paired ground-truth comparisons in Fig. 3 indicate GLOW-FM offers favorable balance among the compared methods, while unpaired examples in Fig. 4 show natural illumination and fewer artifacts; additional examples are provided in Appendix G. 4.4. Ablation Study Comparison of one-step objectives. Tab. 5 compares TVM with MeanFlow [12], ConsistencyFM [63] and No-TVM (standard Flow Matching [30, 31]), with all other experimental settings held fixed. We additionally evaluate No-TVM at 25 NFEs. Among the matched TAESD one-step variants, TVM achieves the strongest overall distortion and perceptual performance. MeanFlow forms its JVP target from the initial-time velocity, whose sample-wise approximation can destabilize training [71]; this may be particularly problematic for LLIE, where the initial state is degraded low-light image. ConsistencyFM enforces velocity-consistent straight flow, which may restrict single full-interval mapping for spatially heterogeneous restoration [9, 63]. TVM instead regularizes the displacement at its predicted terminal state, aligning the one-step mapping with the velocity near the enhanced endpoint [71]. Effect of training-set size. Fig. 5 isolates the effect of data availability by training GLOW-FM on progressively larger LSD-DLL subsets while keeping the architecture and training protocol fixed. Increasing the training set from approximately 0.2K to 3.0K image pairs improves PSNR monotonically from 16.8 to 20.3 dB and MUSIQ from 34.5 to 36.0. This trend supports our data-limited interpretation of the LOL-v1 distortion results and is consistent with prior observations that flow-based models benefit strongly from additional training data [72]. Effect of latent representation. Tab. 5 further evaluates the effect of the latent representation on GLOW-FM performance. We compare the proposed TAESD latent representation against larger SD-VAE and direct pixel-space variant while keeping the velocity network fixed. TAESD achieves better PSNR, SSIM, and NIQE with nearly an order of magnitude less computation, whereas SD-VAE achieves better LPIPS and MUSIQ at substantially higher computational and parameter costs. Additional autoencoder-reconstruction analysis is provided in Appendix E. We further compare against pixel-space variant that removes the latent representation entirely. Despite requiring significantly more computation, direct pixel-space modeling produces substantially weaker distortion and perceptual quality. These results indicate that the proposed latent-space formulation is not only computationally advantageous but also improves enhancement quality, suggesting that the compact TAESD representation provides an effective latent space for LLIE. 5. Conclusion Low-light image enhancement remains challenging because noise, color shifts, and information loss make faithful restoration ambiguous. Although recent generative LLIE methods have reduced sampling cost, combining single-step inference, low overall computation, and robust performance across real-world conditions remains challenging. In this work, we address this challenge with GLOW-FM, an efficient generative LLIE framework based on one-step latent flow matching. By combining efficiency-aware latent flow matching with Terminal Velocity Matching, GLOW-FM enables single-NFE enhancement while preserving generative priors for realistic restoration. Experiments show competitive quality, improved efficiency, and state-of-the-art cross-dataset generalization, suggesting practical direction for robust and efficient generative low-light enhancement.

We retained the official architecture, optimization settings, and training schedule, modifying only the dataset configuration as necessary. For LOL-v1, we used the official pretrained weights released by the respective authors whenever available. TFFormer was the only exception: because no official LOL-v1 checkpoint was available, we also trained it from scratch on the LOL-v1 training set. Unless otherwise stated, the training details below describe our retraining on LSD-DLL and UHD-LOL4K, and all models were trained using NVIDIA H100 GPUs. TFFormer. We trained separate TFFormer model from scratch on each of LSD-DLL, UHD-LOL4K, and LOL-v1. TFFormer was optimized using an Adam optimizer with hyperparameters β1 = 0.9 and β2 = 0.99. We set the initial learning rate to 104 and adjusted it after 100,000 steps using PyTorchs ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler [43]. We trained each model for 300,000 steps on single GPU using batch size of 24 and 128128 RGB patches. Additionally, we used low-light regularization coefficient of λR = 0.2 for the combined reconstruction and luminancechrominance objective. HVI-CIDNet. HVI-CIDNet was trained with the Adam optimizer (β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999) and 256 256 input crops using single GPU for 1,000 epochs with batch size of 4. The initial learning rate was 104 and is then steadily decreased to 1107 using cosine annealing scheme [33] during training. We used the default HVI-CIDNet data augmentation pipeline, consisting of random cropping, random horizontal flipping, and random vertical flipping. Retinexformer. We trained Retinexformer using the Adam optimizer with β1 =0.9 and β2 =0.999, an initial learning rate of 2104 then steadily decreased to 1106 by the cosine annealing scheme [33]. Training is set for 2.5105 iterations. We train with batch size 8 on randomly cropped 128128 patches, and apply data augmentation of random rotation and flipping. PyDiff. PyDiff was trained from scratch using random 192288 crops, horizontal flipping, and brightness augmentation with factor sampled from [0.5,1.5]. We used Adam with an initial learning rate of 104 and batch size of 8 per GPU. The learning rate was multiplied by 0.5 after 50k, 75k, 100k, 150k, and 200k iterations. Training was conducted for 500k iterations using the official 2,000-step linear diffusion schedule, with variance endpoints of 106 and 102. WCDM. WCDM was trained from scratch using random 256 256 crops and batch size of 12. The model was optimized with Adam using learning rate of 104 and zero weight decay. The learning rate was multiplied by 0.8 every 5,000 iterations, and an exponential moving average with decay of 0.999 was maintained during training. Training was conducted for 1,000 epochs, following the official training schedule. We used the official 200-step linear diffusion schedule with variance endpoints of 104 and 2102. ReDDiT. For each of LSD-DLL and UHD-LOL4K, we followed the ReDDiT progressive-distillation procedure. We first trained the required dataset-specific GSAD teacher from scratch for 750 epochs in FP32 using random 96 96 crops. Training was performed across eight GPUs with batch size of 8 per GPU, yielding an effective batch size of 64. We used Adam with learning rate of 104. The teacher objective combined the ℓ1 reconstruction loss and the GSAD structural loss with weights of 10 and 1, respectively, and employed 500-step linear diffusion schedule. Starting from the dataset-specific teacher, we first trained an eight-step ReDDiT model and then progressively distilled it into four-step and two-step students. Each distillation stage was trained for 5,000 iterations using random 9696 crops, batch size of 16, Adam with learning rate of 104, and an exponential moving average with decay of 0.9999. The ReDDiT stages used fine-grained diffusion-time discretization of =512 with linear β-schedule whose endpoints were 104 and 2102. Multinex. We trained Multinex using the Adam optimizer with cosine annealing learning-rate schedule [33] that decays from 2 104 to 1 106. Multinex is trained from scratch for 150K iterations with batch size of 8 and patch size of 256256. The extended architecture ablation in Tab. 7 first evaluates the effect of the latent autoencoder on end-to-end enhancement. Compared with the SD-VAE-based variant, the TAESD-based GLOW-FM achieves higher PSNR and SSIM and lower NIQE while reducing the computational cost from 471 to 48 GFLOPs and the parameter count from 205M to 124M. The SD-VAE variant achieves lower LPIPS and higher MUSIQ, reflecting different distortionperception trade-off. To separate transport-model error from the reconstruction error introduced by the frozen autoencoder, we additionally evaluate direct target reconstruction, x0 = D(E(x0)), for TAESD and SD-VAE across the three paired benchmarks. This setting represents the performance obtained when the target encoding is recovered exactly and therefore provides useful reconstruction reference, but not strict bound on the output of GLOW-FM. In particular, PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS measure correspondence with the paired target, whereas the no-reference metrics NIQE and MUSIQ assess perceptual image statistics and may improve even when reconstruction fidelity decreases. We therefore report NIQE and MUSIQ only as complementary diagnostics. As shown in Tab. 8, direct TAESD reconstruction achieves higher PSNR and SSIM and lower LPIPS than SD-VAE reconstruction on all three datasets. Fig. 9 studies the effect of gradually introducing the TVM objective during training. We compare the proposed warmup-ramp schedule against variant trained without TVM warmup. Without TVM warmup, the TVM objective is introduced before the flow-matching model has learned meaningful low-to-normal-light transport. As result, the displacement objective is optimized with respect to an immature velocity field, leading the optimization toward an inferior solution. In contrast, the proposed warmup schedule allows the flow-matching objective to first establish reliable transport before introducing the TVM objective, resulting in improved PSNR and substantially better NIQE at convergence. Tab. 15 reports end-to-end inference latency and peak memory usage. All measurements use batch size one and report latency averaged over 100 timed inferences following 20 warm-up iterations. GPU measurements were obtained on single NVIDIA H100 at resolutions from 256256 to 40964096. We additionally evaluate 10241024 inference on an Apple M4 Max using ONNX with Arm SME/SME2 acceleration. SME is an Armv9-A instruction-set extension designed to accelerate matrix and vector processing [2]. On the H100, GLOW-FM-S achieves the lowest latency and peak allocated memory across all evaluated resolutions. At high resolutions, all GLOW-FM variants are substantially faster and require less GPU memory than the compared generative methods. Under Arm SME/SME2 execution, all GLOW-FM variants also achieve lower latency than the competing methods.
